strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear articulation of why neural approaches improve over combinatorial optimization for ad hoc network topology generation
Comprehensive integration of domain knowledge through engineered features (antenna sectors, link angles) and constraint-aware loss terms demonstrating solid problem understanding
CAM tokens provide a reasonable architectural contribution for improving global graph control through learnable modulation, clearly described with mathematical rigor
Ablation studies (Tables 1 and 3) validate the contribution of architectural components and loss terms
Practical network evolution approach using partial diffusion to handle node mobility without full reconfiguration
Transparent implementation details including hardware, hyperparameters, and learning rates
weaknesses: Critical experimental limitation: Full evaluation only on 16-node networks; 32-node testing abandoned without resolution, severely limiting scalability validation and practical applicability claims

Constraint satisfaction incomplete: 12.31% node saturation (vs ~0%), 98.65% parity (vs ~100%), and reliance on Algorithm 2 post-processing (250ms) undermines claims of learned compliance; total system time (730ms) is non-negligible

Insufficient baseline comparison: Only compares against authors' own 'Standard GT' implementation; missing comparisons with the greedy Algorithm 1 it aims to replace and other DDPM/graph generation methods from related work
Performance metrics concerning: Generated topologies underperform targets (1.60 vs 1.72 Mbps throughput) while using 13% more links and producing 66% higher antenna saturation than target datasets

Incomplete ablation studies: No isolated CAM token ablation (Table 1 removes both CAM and handcrafted features); marginal improvements shown (98.12%→99.13% connectivity); claims about oversmoothing reduction unvalidated
Insufficient validation of proposed contributions: Network evolution algorithm (Section 4.3) introduced but entirely untested despite being claimed as key contribution; no motion experiments

Technical clarity issues: Noise schedule transition matrix m inadequately explained; binary edge formulation oversimplified for complex physical constraints; Equation 11 cosine loss formulation unmotivated

Reproducibility and generalization concerns: No public dataset (claims 'thousands of random sets' without specificity); no code release mentioned; no confidence intervals or statistical rigor (variance, significance tests); training convergence behavior not reported

Limited novelty: DDPM for graph generation is established; graph transformers standard; CAM tokens build incrementally on existing FiLM/attention mechanisms; mainly an application to specialized domain
Narrow applicability: Specialized to directional antenna ad hoc networks with unclear practical advantage over existing methods given still-required post-processing and constraint violations

strengths: Well-motivated application domain addressing a real computational challenge in network topology optimization
Practical integration of constraint handling through problem-specific loss terms and features
Temporal network evolution mechanism that addresses node mobility in ad hoc networks
Demonstrates technical feasibility of applying DDPMs to network topology generation with reasonable inference times
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: CAM tokens are incremental modifications combining cross-attention and FiLM modulation (existing techniques); core DDPM approach is standard
Severely incomplete evaluation: only one baseline (Standard GT) with no comparison to the target greedy algorithm or other graph generation methods (MolGAN, DIGRESS, etc.)
Missing critical experimental details: dataset size/construction procedure, training/validation/test split methodology, loss term weighting scheme, and convergence analysis prevent reproducibility
Post-hoc correction algorithm (Algorithm 2) is essential for operational use, undermining claims that the method solves the problem—suggests constraints are not genuinely learned
Inadequate testing scope: only 16-node networks thoroughly evaluated; 32-node experiments abandoned 'for technical reasons'; no demonstration of scalability
Incomplete network evolution algorithm: no empirical evaluation, no theoretical justification, and potential bias from using previous topology as initialization

Model violates constraints despite explicit penalties: 12.31% saturated nodes vs. ~10% target, 98.65% parity vs. 99%+ claimed performance; Table 3 shows parity loss is 'mandatory', suggesting fundamental misalignment
No statistical significance testing or error bars; minimal improvements from proposed CAM tokens over baselines (Table 1: 99.13% vs. 99.07% connectivity; differences may not be significant)
Poor presentation: Algorithm 1 informally described; relationship between greedy algorithm and DDPM learning objective never formally established; critical technical details vague or missing
Insufficient analysis: no failure case discussion, no visualization of generated topologies, no ablation on loss term weights, no theoretical justification for design choices

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem: generating topologies for directional antenna networks is novel and addresses real computational challenges
Comprehensive constraint handling: domain-specific loss terms and features effectively improve adherence to physical constraints (parity: 98.65% vs 67.07% baseline)
Demonstrates clear improvements over baseline: outperforms standard graph transformer on connectivity (99.13% vs 98.12%) and saturated nodes (12.31% vs 17.08%)
Engineering maturity: includes practical post-processing, network evolution algorithm, and thoughtful architecture design for the problem domain
Clear problem formulation and motivation: well-articulated case for why deep learning is appropriate for this application
weaknesses: Severely limited evaluation scope: experiments restricted to 16-node networks; authors state they 'could not generate a full dataset and test set of 32-node-sets' due to technical reasons, undermining generalization claims

Inadequate baseline comparisons: only compared to standard graph transformer, not to VAE [5,6], GAN [7,8], or autoregressive [9] graph generation methods; no computational comparison with the O(m²) greedy algorithm

Post-processing requirement undermines core claims: Algorithm 2 requires 250ms (54% of generation time), but paper doesn't report how often it modifies outputs or percentage of graphs violating constraints
Poor reproducibility: dataset size and source not specified; no code availability mentioned; hyperparameter choices unexplained (10 blocks, 50 steps, learning rates 1e-4 to 1e-7)

Persistent performance gaps indicate incomplete learning: generated topologies have 13.3% more links (49.74 vs 43.90), 66% higher saturated antennas (16.19% vs 9.74%), and 7% lower throughput than targets
Limited technical novelty: DDPM formulation largely follows DIGRESS [13]; CAM tokens are straightforward adaptation of standard cross-attention plus established FiLM modulation [27,28]
Network evolution algorithm (Section 4.3) lacks validation: no ablation study, no comparison with full retraining, no evaluation on real dynamic scenarios
Missing isolated ablation for CAM tokens: Table 1 shows NetDiff vs no features vs baseline GT, but not CAM contribution alone
Unclear technical details: Equation 1 product notation contradicts stated goal of modeling edge interdependence; Section 4.3 lacks theoretical justification for noise initialization strategy
No real-world or simulation validation: throughput computed via simulation only; claims about practical deployment unvalidated; no network simulator (e.g., NS-3) experiments

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear articulation of why generative models are appropriate for directional antenna topology generation
Comprehensive system design addressing joint topology-parity generation, constraint satisfaction, and temporal updates for mobility
ACAM token mechanism with unsoftmaxed cross-attention shows empirical improvements (saturation reduced from 11.62% to 7.05%)
Practical partial diffusion approach achieves 3-5× speedup for topology updates under mobility
Solid experimental methodology with multiple baselines, ablation studies, and detailed constraint satisfaction metrics
Good reproducibility details on training hyperparameters, architecture specifications, and random seeds
Clear presentation with effective visualizations illustrating the generation process
weaknesses: Partial diffusion mechanism lacks rigorous theoretical justification; the empirical observation that 'edge variations match intermediate diffusion states' is not formally validated or analyzed for error accumulation

ACAM token contribution is incremental; removing softmax from attention is presented as enabling 'counting' but lacks theoretical analysis of why this is superior to alternative global encoding schemes

Reproducibility severely limited by reliance on proprietary antenna patterns, propagation models, and attenuation laws that cannot be disclosed; makes dataset reproduction impossible despite providing neural network details

Narrow experimental scope: main results on 16-node networks only; 32-node results in appendix show significant performance degradation (saturation 14.08% vs 9.91% target); no evaluation across different network types or deployment scenarios

Post-processing correction algorithm (Algorithm 2) still required to enforce hard constraints, undermining claims of generating valid topologies; model outputs are not production-ready without correction
Loss function designs (Eq. 14-16) appear ad-hoc with hand-crafted thresholds and operators; Table 4 shows essential contribution but limited ablation on alternative formulations

Evaluation limited in rigor: throughput upper bound excludes dynamic routing and multi-channel scheduling; target values come from same reference solver as training data, not independent validation; limited uncertainty quantification; no failure case analysis

Limited novelty: core DDPM framework follows Vignac et al. (2023a) closely; ACAM is essentially cross-attention + FiLM (known techniques); partial diffusion is straightforward timestep interpolation; primary contribution is application-specific rather than methodological
Incomplete comparisons: TopoFormer mentioned but not directly compared; no comparison with traditional optimization or recent GNN-based optimizers; no generalization analysis on distribution shift

Scalability concerns: networks only up to 32 nodes in detail; 40+ nodes mentioned to require partitioning but not evaluated; limited ablation on architectural choices (why use 1 ACAM token when 16 reduces saturation by 0.8%?)

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear practical relevance for directional antenna network optimization under multiple constraints
Technically sound application of discrete diffusion framework appropriately adapted for the domain
Practical partial diffusion mechanism for incremental topology updates under node mobility
Comprehensive ablations demonstrating contributions of CAM/ACAM tokens and individual loss terms
Honest discussion of limitations including data generation challenges, post-processing requirements, and network size scalability
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: closely follows DiGress (Vignac et al. 2023a) with modest ACAM contribution (removing softmax from cross-attention for 'counting'). Modest performance gains (7.98% to 7.05% saturation) do not justify claimed innovation
Heavy reliance on post-processing correction (Algorithm 2) to enforce hard constraints suggests the neural model does not learn constraints end-to-end, undermining claims of learning global coherence
Highly specialized domain (directional antennas, sector constraints, bipartite parity) with unclear generalizability to other graph generation tasks, limiting impact for a broad ML venue

Evaluation severely limited to 16-node networks; 32-node results show degradation (saturation 14.08% vs 9.91% target, throughput 5.90 vs 6.26 target). No evaluation beyond 32 nodes or on real-world networks
Missing key baseline comparison with TopoFormer (Marcoccia et al., 2025), identified as addressing similar problems. Provided excuse is unconvincing
Purely synthetic evaluation with no real-world validation on actual hardware, antenna patterns, or field deployments. Throughput metrics are theoretical upper bounds excluding dynamic routing

Data generation quality and diversity unclear: relies on expensive simulation with unexplained heuristic fallback fraction, proprietary simulation parameters omitted, making reproducibility impossible
Partial diffusion evaluation lacks rigor: 'continuity' metric undefined (what does 33% mean?), claimed 3.3-5x speedup lacks quantitative details, no comparison with standard regeneration
Reproducibility concerns: single random seed, many unexplained hyperparameters, proprietary simulation dependencies, no code/dataset availability, incomplete architecture specification
No theoretical justification for why unsoftmaxed cross-attention specifically solves global cardinality matching. Ablation shows ACAM helps but doesn't isolate specific mechanisms
Paper attempts to cover too much ground (topology generation, parity assignment, ACAM, partial diffusion, losses), diluting focus and obscuring core novelty
Inference time (450ms) not contextualized against baselines or real-time requirements; unclear if competitive with baselines or simpler methods

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear practical relevance to directional wireless networks; problem formulation clearly articulated with good motivation for generative modeling approach
Novel partial diffusion mechanism for topology updates under mobility is creative and well-motivated; 3.3-5× speedup with improved continuity demonstrates practical value
ACAM tokens effectively improve global graph coherence through unsoftmaxed cross-attention; empirical results (Tables 1, 3) show consistent improvements in constraint satisfaction
Joint topology-parity generation addresses limitation of concurrent work (TopoFormer) by avoiding expensive post-processing
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with clear ablations showing component contributions; strong improvements over VAE and diffusion baselines
Domain-specific features and loss terms well-motivated and empirically validated (Table 4 demonstrates necessity)
Good reproducibility: training details, hyperparameters, random seeds, and hardware specifications provided
Clear presentation with helpful visualizations (Figures 2, 5) and appropriate impact statement addressing ethical considerations
weaknesses: Post-processing requirement (Algorithm 2) undermines claims about learning constraints; results conflate model performance with correction algorithm performance; unclear if inference timing includes correction overhead
ACAM contribution is relatively incremental—primarily removing softmax from attention; claim that unsoftmaxed aggregation enables counting lacks rigorous justification
Limited novelty of core components: base approach directly follows DiGress with standard discrete diffusion and graph transformers; most contributions are domain-specific applications
Training data distribution shift not analyzed: quasi-exhaustive search + heuristic fallback creates optimization oracle distribution potentially mismatched with deployment scenarios
Insufficient analysis of ACAM mechanism: missing ablations on token count, attention function choice, and visualizations of learned global features

Limited experimental scope: evaluation restricted to 16-32 node networks; 40+ nodes require partitioning; no comparison with TopoFormer (even if different problem); no real-world deployment validation
Design choices unjustified: no ablation on diffusion steps (50), transformer blocks (5), or feature dimension (32)
Missing ablations: number of ACAM tokens, attention similarity function, loss term weighting strategy
Partial diffusion evaluation limited to realistic trajectory patterns; no adversarial perturbations; continuity metrics (33-39%) lack practical interpretation
